label: GPT-6.1 Terra
output:
**Dear Kelechi,**

First of all, please appreciate the fact that I have bought a stamp for you. An actual stamp. You laughed at me at my birthday and said that if I was serious about you becoming a maths teacher, I should put it in a proper letter. You thought you had won because you know how much I like a voice note. Well, here we are. I hope you are reading this on the train, looking very important in your quantity surveyor clothes.

I’ve been thinking about what you said that night. Not just the part where you complained about your job for the hundredth time, although yes, I was listening. You said every day feels like the same spreadsheet. Nine years at the same firm in Croydon is a long time to feel like that. And I keep remembering what you said on your birthday too: “I just want to do something that matters before 40.”

Now, before you roll your eyes, I’m not saying your work doesn’t matter. Buildings cost money, and somebody has to stop people spending it anyhow. I’m also not saying you should march into the office tomorrow and resign because your friend has written you a dramatic letter. Please don’t do that and then come to my house asking for jollof.

I’m saying I think you could be a really good teacher, and I think it’s worth finding out whether you would enjoy it.

You’ve always had a way of explaining things. At Unilag, before exams, half our hostel in Moremi would somehow end up around you while you worked through maths problems. And you never made anyone feel stupid for not getting it the first time. You’d find another way to explain, make somebody laugh, and carry on until it made sense. You got an A in further maths, yes, but plenty of people are good at maths and can’t explain it to save their lives. That’s not your problem.

Look at my nephew at Christmas. He was fed up with fractions, and you started dividing jollof rice between plates as if you were sharing out an inheritance. The boy still talks about it. He wasn’t scared of getting the answer wrong with you. That patience, and the way you can make someone comfortable enough to try, would count for a lot in a classroom.

I see what a difference it makes when someone finally gets something they thought they couldn’t do. Last month, one of my Year 11 boys, Damola, had been wrestling with simultaneous equations for about three weeks. We tried them this way and that way, and then one lesson it clicked. He looked at the board and shouted, “Is that all??” The whole class clapped.

I laughed because, after three weeks, excuse me, sir, it was not *all* five minutes ago. But he was so pleased with himself. I went home smiling about it. You don’t get that particular kind of moment from checking somebody else’s costings, even if the spreadsheet is beautifully formatted.

And schools do need people. At mine in Peckham, we have about 1,100 pupils, and two Year 9 maths groups have had a supply teacher covering them since September. I keep thinking how much it would help those pupils to have a teacher they can get to know and rely on. That isn’t a guilt trip for you to personally come and rescue Peckham, please. I’m just telling you what things look like from where I stand.

But let me also tell you the parts that won’t appear in the cheerful picture in your head. Teaching is hard. The marking can feel endless. Behaviour some days is proper wahala, and there are afternoons when a lesson you spent ages planning falls completely flat. You can care about the children and still need five minutes alone before you speak to another human being.

When I started in 2019, I cried in the car park twice in my first term. Twice! I’m telling you because I don’t want to sell you a fantasy and have you call me a liar by October. It got better as I learned what I was doing, got to know my classes and stopped expecting myself to have every answer. There are still difficult weeks, but there are enough good moments, like Damola’s, to remind me why I’m there.

I know money is a real question too. The route I’m talking about is the salaried training route, so you would be paid while you train. It’s one year, starting in September 2027. I know there would still be a pay drop in that first year, and I’m not going to pretend holidays and a pension magically pay your bills. You’d need to look at the actual figures and decide what works for you. The pay goes up, and the holidays and pension are worth considering too, but you should ask the people running the training all the awkward questions. You are very good at those.

And before you tell me you’re too old to start again at 34, please rest. A woman in my department started at 41. You would bring nine years of working life with you, not turn up having forgotten everything you’ve ever done. There’s time to try something different if that’s what you decide you want.

So here is my very unreasonable demand: come to the open evening with me.

It’s **Thursday 19 November 2026, at 6pm**, at the training partnership in Lewisham. Applications for next September open soon, so it’s a good chance to hear how the salaried route works, ask about the pay and training, and see what you think. I’ll come with you. Afterwards we can find food and you can tell me every reason I’m wrong.

You don’t have to sign anything. You don’t even have to decide that night. Just come and have a proper look. If you hear it all and decide teaching isn’t for you, I’ll accept that. I might still tease you about your spreadsheets, but I was going to do that anyway.

I’ve known you since Unilag, and I know how funny and patient you are, even if you will deny the patient part when somebody is walking slowly in front of you. I’ve seen the way you help people understand things without making a big show of it. I can picture you doing that for a class full of teenagers, and I think some of them would be lucky to have you.

Think about it, my friend. And please let me know about the 19th before I start sending you a second letter by recorded delivery.

**Your friend**
